Absolute right of inheritance

By: Annalise Lubbe | Production

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
Private wills will come under the spotlight in a ‘world first’ matter when the ConCourt have to decide on the ‘absolute right of inheritance’ for adopted children and ‘male only’ heirs. We

Unique Selling Point:
Private wills – as opposed to charitable trusts – are considered sacrosanct, not only in South Africa but the world over. As long as a person is of “sound mind” and not financially responsible for any minor children, they are legally entitled to pass on their assets to whoever they please and can disinherit on a whim. But in a constitutional dispensation this is not an “absolute right” and must be balanced against equality, it has been argued in two matters that will now come before the Constitutional Court in February.

Summary:
The first case involves the inheritance rights of adult adoptees. In the other, five sisters have challenged a “males only” clause in their great-grandfather’s will. Both challenges started in the Cape Town high court, but were unsuccessful. Then the Supreme Court of Appeal (SCA) failed to come to their aid. But the ConCourt has consolidated the two cases and directed the parties to submit arguments on why it should grant leave to appeal as well as the merits of both matters.

There are very few grounds on which to challenge a private will in South Africa (and in fact worldwide). Essentially a person can leave their money and property to whoever they want.
Usually challenges are made on allegations that the person was unduly influenced, or was not sane at the time of writing the will. But, as far as we know - and what the papers say in these two matters - the “constitutionality” of a private will has never been tested before.

The argument in both these cases is that the right of someone to leave their money to whoever they wish is not “absolute” and should be balanced against equality provisions in the Bill of Rights and the Constitution.


Further information:
Adopted children case:
David Wilkinson and his sister Amanda Truter are from Port Elizabeth. Dulcie Harper, who was unable to have children, adopted them as newborns in the 1950s. In 1953, before Harper adopted the babies, her father Louis John Druiff died. In a trust deed and will, Druiff left his estate in equal shares to his four children and, on their deaths, their children. Harper died in December 2017. She was the last of Druiff’s four children to die. Her death sparked a legal battle between Wilkinson and Truter and their cousins about who was entitled to inherit Harper’s share of her father’s estate.

The cousins, the natural children of Harper’s siblings, claimed that Wilkinson and Truter, as adopted children, were not entitled to the inheritance because Druiff only intended “blood descendents” to inherit. Wilkinson and Truter argued that this interpretation was incorrect, resulted in unfair discrimination and was not in line with the “spirit, purpose and object of the bill of rights and the constitution”.

The appeal court judges were divided. Judge Mahube Betty Molemela said in a minority judgment that Druiff had used the term “any child”. There was no reason why this should lead to the conclusion that he intended to disinherit children adopted after his death. She noted that Druiff was aware, before his death, that Harper was considering adoption.

But the majority judgment, penned by judge Visvanathan Ponnan, highlighted the constitution's protection of a person’s right to property, including the right to dispose of their assets as they wish upon their death. “The fundamental question is the extent to which freedom of testation must yield to freedom from unfair discrimination,” the judges said. “Inroads into freedom of testation are not to be made lightly. No one has a right to inherit. The terms of the trust deed were certain and valid and not contrary to public policy at the time.”

The adopted siblings’ lawyers said the case raises “important constitutional issues".
"The net result is that adopted children are being discriminated against solely on the basis of their birth and status, which is a contravention of the constitution … There is no authoritative pronouncement on the issue. None of the authorities deal with private trust in the present constitutional dispensation,” they said. They argued that the appeal court failed to take into account “radical developments of law” concerning adopted children and that “public policy” is not a static concept. “Any finding which results in adoptive children not being on equal footing would today fall foul of public policy and the equality clause in the constitution.”

Wilkinson and Truter are adopted children (now adults) of Harper who want to claim from her fathers’ (Druiff) estate. In his will he provided that his children and their children can inherit.
In the Western Cape High Court, the court ruled against them as did the majority of judges in the SCA. They highlighted the protection of the Constitution of a person's right to property including the right to dispose of their assets as they wish upon their death.
“The fundamental question is the extent to which freedom of testation, must yield to freedom from unfair discrimination,” they said. “Inroads into freedom of testation are not to be made lightly. Noone has a right to inherit. The terms of the trust deed were certain and valid and not contrary to public policy at the time.”

But in a minority judgment, Judge Mahube Molemela, aid Druiff had used the term “any child”. There was no reason why this should lead to the conclusion that he intended to disinherit children adopted after his own death. It was this minority judgment that led to the Legal Aid Board taking up the case on behalf of adopted children on appeal to the Constitutional Court. They had run out of money and were not going to pursue it. I would guess from that, that the Legal Aid Board believes it has a strong case and one which is deserving of Concourt scrutiny. Lawyers acting for the adopted siblings, have submitted the case raises “important Constitutional issues”.

They say: “The net result is that adopted children are being discriminated against solely on the basis of their birth and status which is a contravention of the Constitution. “There is no authoritative pronouncement on the issue. None of the authorities deal with private trust in the present Constitutional dispensation. “ They argue that the SCA failed to take into account “radical developments of law” concerning adopted children and that “public policy” is not a static concept. “Any finding which results in adoptive children not being on equal footing would today fall foul of public policy and the equality clause in the Constitution.”

This case really comes down to interpretation of a will (which did not specifically preclude adopted children) but even if it did, is that permissible today?

The “men only” case
In the second matter, sisters Trudene Forword, Annelie Jordaan, Elna Slabber, Kalene Roux and Surina Serfontein claimed unfair discrimination after being disinherited because the will their great-grandparents drafted in 1902 specified that only “male heirs” could inherit their farms and other properties. Their father Kalvyn de Jager died in 2015 having had only daughters.

Their male cousins then laid claim to the properties, admitting that it may be “unfair discrimination” but that it is justified and “freedom of testation should take precedence”.
In written arguments, lawyers for the sisters said a will that is inimical (obstruct, unfriendly) to constitutional values, that is contrary to public policy, is not enforceable. “While the law of succession offers a testator very wide freedom, this is limited by common law, statute and the constitution," they argued.

“For example, if a property owner were to conclude a contract with an estate agent which permits the agent to only market and sell the property to persons of a particular race or gender, it stands to reason that such contract would be unenforceable on the basis of breach of public policy.

“If there is to be a blanket acceptance that freedom of testation trumps equality in all cases of out-and-out disinheritance, the result would be a ‘constitution-free zone’ created under the guise of freedom to testation.”

But lawyers for the cousins say neither the interim constitution nor the final constitution reaches backwards to invalidate actions taken before they commenced. “It is significant that at the Supreme Court of Appeal, the counsel [for the sisters] had to concede that they are contending for a ‘world first’ in the sense that no foreign jurisdiction has outlawed discrimination in the form of out-and-out disinheritance in a private will.”

They also argued that this was not the case to decide a constitutional issue. “Over the past 117 years, the family has arranged their affairs in accordance with the will,” they said. “Some of the properties have been sold - it will be difficult to unscramble these transactions.” They said their clients were not able to justify the discrimination because of the passage of time and that it was impossible to establish what benefits were distributed to females in lieu of property in the past. “There is also the spectre of a Pandora’s box of litigation regarding private wills, in which the testators’ last wishes are second-guessed by a court, which might have little inkling as to why,” they said.

The five sisters are challenging their grand grandfathers will which left properties only to male sheirs (back in 1902). Their father only had girls (them) so they are now disinherited because of that and their male cousins stand to gain (the male children of their uncle).
They lost in the Western Cape High Court and the SCA did not grant leave to appeal (no reasons).

This case is probably less winnable. While it might be contrary to public policy and the constitution in the present day, it wasn’t back then. But the court may pronounce on this issue without fiddling with the terms of the will - ie it may say that in the present day this would be unconstitutional meaning that a present day testator may have to be more cautious about who he leaves his money to - and may have to give sound reasons for disinheritance - in order to avoid a “constitutional challenge” by disgruntled potential heirs. So either way they are important matters.

The court has issued directions that argument in both matters be filed on the leave to appeal issue and the merits. So that means both will be argued. It is possible that after hearing both, they may not grant leave to appeal! But that essentially means that they are not interested in addressing the merits of the matter. But my sense is they want to rule - one way or another - on the Constitutionality issue.

Press Release:


The Absolute Right to Inherit
Private wills are untouchable – as long as you are not financially responsible for minor children, you can pass on your assets or disinherit whomever you choose. But what if discrimination on grounds of being female, or adopted, excludes children in a family from what they believe should be theirs? In a legal first, the Constitutional Court is considering whether all children in a family have an equal right to inherit in a constitutional dispensation that promotes equality.
Producer: Annalise Lubbe | Presenter: Claire Mawisa


Script:


Final script: Absolute Right To Inheritance
Duration: 9 Minutes

V/O South Africa has a progressive bill of rights. Now, for the first time in history and, in two separate cases, our Constitutional Court will decide if the right to equality trumps the right to freedom of testation or the right to choose who should inherit our assets.

V/O Amanda Truter is 62 years old and lives in Port Elizabeth. She was adopted as a newborn in the 1950s by Dulcie and Michael Wilkinson, who also adopted a second child, David.

Claire Mawisa: How did you find out that you were adopted?

Amanda Truter - I was very young. My mom sat me down in the lounge in Grahamstown where we lived and she said she wants to tell me something. She said you have been adopted. She said your mommy and daddy could not keep you but now we are your new mom and dad. You know how much we love you.

V/O Dulcie had tried for several years to fall pregnant and had two miscarriages by the age of 30. She was one of four children: both her sisters and her brother were already blessed with their own offspring. Dulcie confided in her father her intention to adopt.

Amanda Truter: My mom said she was very very close to him. Her mother died when she was 8 years old.

V/O Although Druiff was aware of his daughter’s intention to adopt, the adoption only took place after his death in 1953. In the Druiff Trust, it is clear that Dulcie’s father made equal provision for all four of his children: on his death, he left his estate in equal shares to his four children and at their death, to their legal descendants.

V/O It had been many years since Dulcie had had that conversation with her father. She was now in her nineties and wanted peace of mind that on her death, her adopted children would inherit her share. She went to see an attorney, Katie Morris, for advice.

Katie Morris: Attorney: The trustees of her father’s trust had advised her that on legal advice that on her death that the share that was due to be paid out to her children would not be paid to her children due to the fact that there are words in the Trust Deed such as ‘descendents’ and ‘issue’ that they deemed not to include the adopted children.

V/O Dulcie had to break the news to her children.

Amanda Truter: I burst into tears. I could not believe it. They say, they did not want to say this, let me know because they knew it would hurt me. The reason I cannot inherit anything from the trust fund is because I am adopted.

V/O Elmarie Neilson is an attorney in Cape Town. She specialises in the legal rights of dopted children.

Elmarie Neilson - Legal Expert: In 1953 when Louis John Druiff executed this trust deed the Children’s Act of 1937 was enforced. And it said that an adopted child for all respect be counted as a natural child except when it came to inheritance. Then adopted children were automatically excluded unless the trust deed or will specifically included them.

Katie Morris: My instructions from Mrs Harper were that her father would not have wanted her children to be treated differently.

Elmarie Neilson: The line of attack for the applicants in the adopted children case was that they were discriminated against on the base of their birth, and they said that the testator knew that she was going to adopt and that therefore the Trust Deed should be amended to include them.

V/O The case was heard in the Western Cape High Court in Cape Town. In a majority ruling the right to freedom of testation won over the right not to be unfairly discriminated against. The applicants were granted leave to appeal the judgment in the Supreme Court of Appeal in Bloemfontein but were once again unsuccessful.

V/O In a statement from the respondents, Dulcie’s blood relatives, they said the two preceding judgments speak for themselves and that it remains a sensitive family matter involving private property and they asked that their right to privacy be respected.

V/O Dulcie died at the age of 94 leaving David and Amanda to continue the legal process.

Up sound

V/O David was ill at the time with a severe form of skin cancer. He was too weak in the end to continue the legal battle. He died on Christmas day last year leaving behind his wife Jean to be his voice.

Claire Mawisa: What was the last month been like?

Jean Wilkinson: It has been hectic sorting out all of his affairs out. By the time he had died he was so sick and so weak he could not really worry about anything like that.

Claire Mawisa: Did David ask you to continue the fight even after he passed away?

Jean Wilkinson: He did actually say that he would like me to carry on with it.

V/O The case caught the attention of the Legal Aid Board, who felt it was in the public interest for it to be heard in the Constitutional Court.

Claire Mawisa: So if you are successful in the ConCourt how would the law change for those adopted children who find themselves in a similar situation?

Katie Morris: This would have a massive effect on interpreting wills and trust deeds in that it will be interpreted more progressively and in favour of adopted children who would then be given more rights than what they previously had in respects to historical deeds and wills.

Amanda Truter: I think it is unfair to be judged because you are adopted. It is discrimination. It is the bottom line. It is.

V/O Discrimination is also at the heart of a second case regarding a will and testament drafted over a century ago.

Link: In 1902 a farmer here in Oudtshoorn stipulated in his will that his children and their future male heirs were entitled to inherit his many farms in the area. But one of his grandsons only had daughters and these daughters have decided to contest that will. And if they win they will inherit this farm.

V/O Carel Johannes Cornelis de Jager had been ruling from the grave for 117 years. When his grandson, Kalvyn de Jager, died in 2015, according to the will, only the male cousins could inherit their uncle’s farm. Kalvyn’s five daughters claimed it was discriminatory and contrary to public policy and appointed James King as their attorney.

James King: Attorney: Ons argument in die hof was dat ons het n reg op gelykheid (Our argument in court is that we have a right to equality) en n reg op waardigheid (and a right to dignity,) en dat die testament diskrimineer (and that the will discriminates) en die kliente se reg op waardigheid en reg op gelykheid aantas (and that the applicants’ right to dignity and equality is affected.) en daarom was dit vir ons nodig om vir die hof te vra (And therefore it was necessary for us to ask the court) om hierdie reg sodanig toe te pas (to apply this right) dat jy nie met jou testament kan doen en met jou bates kan diskrimineer soos wat jy wil nie. (in order that one is not allowed to discriminate in your will and do with your assets as you wish.)

Elmarie Neilsons: The other line of attack that the 5 sisters had in court was that the cultures, the norms the laws, and the new constitution have changed and that public policy says that discrimination is absolutely unacceptable and that they should now be counted among the heirs.

V/O They too lost their case in both the Western Cape High Court and the Supreme Court of Appeal but they have been granted permission to state their case in the Constitutional Court as it is a matter of public interest.

James King: As die 5 susters suksesvol is met die saak (If the five sisters are successful with the case,) gaan die testament met ander woorde verander word (the will, in other words, will be changed,) en gaan die woorde ‘’seuns’ vervang word met die woorde ‘kinders’ (and the words “sons” will be replaced with the words “children”,) wat dan ook die 5 dogters insluit en dan behoort Kalvyn de Jager se 5 dogters die plaas te erf. (which will then also include the five daughters and then Kalvyn de Jager’s five daughters ought to inherit the farm.)

Link: So we requested an interview with the five sisters and initially they agreed and so we came to Oudtshoorn. But at the last minute they had a change of heart and did not want to go on camera citing that they would rather wait for the law to take its course.

V/O In a written statement, they said: “The will in question is outdated according to our new Constitution.”

V/O In the male cousins response, they said that the relationship with the applicants is emotional, and spiritually unhealthy, and they do not want to complicate it any further. They also said that publication by any media before the ConCourt hearing could influence public opinion and the judicial process. Furthermore, they believe that the judicial process must take its course independently.

Elmarie Neilson: In the case of the 5 sisters, if they succeed in the concourt then the clause that discriminated against them will have to fall away. In the case of the adopted children, if they win in the Constitutional Court then the trustees of the trust deed will have to treat the adopted children on exactly the same basis as they treat the natural children.

Claire Mawisa: How have the last few years affected your life at all?

Amanda Truter: A lot. Mentally, a lot. It has. There has to be a voice somewhere. I am not a brave person so it is a little squeaky voice saying something must be done.
___________________________________________________________________________________________________________________________________________________________
Promos
1.In the 1950’s the law wasn’t clear about adopted children and their inheritance, but could a ConCourt judgment change all this giving them equal rights to natural born children?

2. A private will is regarded as sacrosanct. But what if discrimination on grounds of sex or birth excludes descendants from their right to inherit what should be theirs?

3. When a farmer dictated in 1902 that women were excluded from inheriting his farms, little did he know that a century later, his great grand-daughters would stand up for their rights.

But the court may pronounce on this issue without fiddling with the terms of the will - ie it may say that in the present day this would be unconstitutional meaning that a present day testator may have to be more cautious about who he leaves his money to - and may have to give sound reasons for disinheritance - in order to avoid a “constitutional challenge” by disgruntled potential heirs. So either way they are important matters. The court has issued directions that argument in both matters be filed on the leave to appeal issue and the merits. So that means both will be argued. It is possible that after hearing both, they may not grant leave to appeal! But that essentially means that they are not interested in addressing the merits of the matter. But my sense is they want to rule - one way or another - on the Constitutionality issue. Carte Blanche HD mihle@combinedartists.co.za 28 February 2020 Press Release: The Absolute Right to Inherit Private wills are untouchable – as long as you are not financially responsible for minor children, you can pass on your assets or disinherit whomever you choose. But what if discrimination on grounds of being female, or adopted, excludes children in a family from what they believe should be theirs? In a legal first, the Constitutional Court is considering whether all children in a family have an equal right to inherit in a constitutional dispensation that promotes equality. Producer: Annalise Lubbe | Presenter: Claire Mawisa Script: Final script: Absolute Right To Inheritance Duration: 9 Minutes V/O South Africa has a progressive bill of rights. Now, for the first time in history and, in two separate cases, our Constitutional Court will decide if the right to equality trumps the right to freedom of testation or the right to choose who should inherit our assets. V/O Amanda Truter is 62 years old and lives in Port Elizabeth. She was adopted as a newborn in the 1950s by Dulcie and Michael Wilkinson, who also adopted a second child, David. Claire Mawisa: How did you find out that you were adopted? Amanda Truter - I was very young. My mom sat me down in the lounge in Grahamstown where we lived and she said she wants to tell me something. She said you have been adopted. She said your mommy and daddy could not keep you but now we are your new mom and dad. You know how much we love you. V/O Dulcie had tried for several years to fall pregnant and had two miscarriages by the age of 30. She was one of four children: both her sisters and her brother were already blessed with their own offspring. Dulcie confided in her father her intention to adopt. Amanda Truter: My mom said she was very very close to him. Her mother died when she was 8 years old. V/O Although Druiff was aware of his daughter’s intention to adopt, the adoption only took place after his death in 1953. In the Druiff Trust, it is clear that Dulcie’s father made equal provision for all four of his children: on his death, he left his estate in equal shares to his four children and at their death, to their legal descendants. V/O It had been many years since Dulcie had had that conversation with her father. She was now in her nineties and wanted peace of mind that on her death, her adopted children would inherit her share. She went to see an attorney, Katie Morris, for advice. Katie Morris: Attorney: The trustees of her father’s trust had advised her that on legal advice that on her death that the share that was due to be paid out to her children would not be paid to her children due to the fact that there are words in the Trust Deed such as ‘descendents’ and ‘issue’ that they deemed not to include the adopted children. V/O Dulcie had to break the news to her children. Amanda Truter: I burst into tears. I could not believe it. They say, they did not want to say this, let me know because they knew it would hurt me. The reason I cannot inherit anything from the trust fund is because I am adopted. V/O Elmarie Neilson is an attorney in Cape Town. She specialises in the legal rights of dopted children. Elmarie Neilson - Legal Expert: In 1953 when Louis John Druiff executed this trust deed the Children’s Act of 1937 was enforced. And it said that an adopted child for all respect be counted as a natural child except when it came to inheritance. Then adopted children were automatically excluded unless the trust deed or will specifically included them. Katie Morris: My instructions from Mrs Harper were that her father would not have wanted her children to be treated differently. Elmarie Neilson: The line of attack for the applicants in the adopted children case was that they were discriminated against on the base of their birth, and they said that the testator knew that she was going to adopt and that therefore the Trust Deed should be amended to include them. V/O The case was heard in the Western Cape High Court in Cape Town. In a majority ruling the right to freedom of testation won over the right not to be unfairly discriminated against. The applicants were granted leave to appeal the judgment in the Supreme Court of Appeal in Bloemfontein but were once again unsuccessful. V/O In a statement from the respondents, Dulcie’s blood relatives, they said the two preceding judgments speak for themselves and that it remains a sensitive family matter involving private property and they asked that their right to privacy be respected. V/O Dulcie died at the age of 94 leaving David and Amanda to continue the legal process. Up sound V/O David was ill at the time with a severe form of skin cancer. He was too weak in the end to continue the legal battle. He died on Christmas day last year leaving behind his wife Jean to be his voice. Claire Mawisa: What was the last month been like? Jean Wilkinson: It has been hectic sorting out all of his affairs out. By the time he had died he was so sick and so weak he could not really worry about anything like that. Claire Mawisa: Did David ask you to continue the fight even after he passed away? Jean Wilkinson: He did actually say that he would like me to carry on with it. V/O The case caught the attention of the Legal Aid Board, who felt it was in the public interest for it to be heard in the Constitutional Court. Claire Mawisa: So if you are successful in the ConCourt how would the law change for those adopted children who find themselves in a similar situation? Katie Morris: This would have a massive effect on interpreting wills and trust deeds in that it will be interpreted more progressively and in favour of adopted children who would then be given more rights than what they previously had in respects to historical deeds and wills. Amanda Truter: I think it is unfair to be judged because you are adopted. It is discrimination. It is the bottom line. It is. V/O Discrimination is also at the heart of a second case regarding a will and testament drafted over a century ago. Link: In 1902 a farmer here in Oudtshoorn stipulated in his will that his children and their future male heirs were entitled to inherit his many farms in the area. But one of his grandsons only had daughters and these daughters have decided to contest that will. And if they win they will inherit this farm. V/O Carel Johannes Cornelis de Jager had been ruling from the grave for 117 years. When his grandson, Kalvyn de Jager, died in 2015, according to the will, only the male cousins could inherit their uncle’s farm. Kalvyn’s five daughters claimed it was discriminatory and contrary to public policy and appointed James King as their attorney. James King: Attorney: Ons argument in die hof was dat ons het n reg op gelykheid (Our argument in court is that we have a right to equality) en n reg op waardigheid (and a right to dignity,) en dat die testament diskrimineer (and that the will discriminates) en die kliente se reg op waardigheid en reg op gelykheid aantas (and that the applicants’ right to dignity and equality is affected.) en daarom was dit vir ons nodig om vir die hof te vra (And therefore it was necessary for us to ask the court) om hierdie reg sodanig toe te pas (to apply this right) dat jy nie met jou testament kan doen en met jou bates kan diskrimineer soos wat jy wil nie. (in order that one is not allowed to discriminate in your will and do with your assets as you wish.) Elmarie Neilsons: The other line of attack that the 5 sisters had in court was that the cultures, the norms the laws, and the new constitution have changed and that public policy says that discrimination is absolutely unacceptable and that they should now be counted among the heirs. V/O They too lost their case in both the Western Cape High Court and the Supreme Court of Appeal but they have been granted permission to state their case in the Constitutional Court as it is a matter of public interest. James King: As die 5 susters suksesvol is met die saak (If the five sisters are successful with the case,) gaan die testament met ander woorde verander word (the will, in other words, will be changed,) en gaan die woorde ‘’seuns’ vervang word met die woorde ‘kinders’ (and the words “sons” will be replaced with the words “children”,) wat dan ook die 5 dogters insluit en dan behoort Kalvyn de Jager se 5 dogters die plaas te erf. (which will then also include the five daughters and then Kalvyn de Jager’s five daughters ought to inherit the farm.) Link: So we requested an interview with the five sisters and initially they agreed and so we came to Oudtshoorn. But at the last minute they had a change of heart and did not want to go on camera citing that they would rather wait for the law to take its course. V/O In a written statement, they said: “The will in question is outdated according to our new Constitution.” V/O In the male cousins response, they said that the relationship with the applicants is emotional, and spiritually unhealthy, and they do not want to complicate it any further. They also said that publication by any media before the ConCourt hearing could influence public opinion and the judicial process. Furthermore, they believe that the judicial process must take its course independently. Elmarie Neilson: In the case of the 5 sisters, if they succeed in the concourt then the clause that discriminated against them will have to fall away. In the case of the adopted children, if they win in the Constitutional Court then the trustees of the trust deed will have to treat the adopted children on exactly the same basis as they treat the natural children. Claire Mawisa: How have the last few years affected your life at all? Amanda Truter: A lot. Mentally, a lot. It has. There has to be a voice somewhere. I am not a brave person so it is a little squeaky voice saying something must be done. ___________________________________________________________________________________________________________________________________________________________ Promos 1.In the 1950’s the law wasn’t clear about adopted children and their inheritance, but could a ConCourt judgment change all this giving them equal rights to natural born children? 2. A private will is regarded as sacrosanct. But what if discrimination on grounds of sex or birth excludes descendants from their right to inherit what should be theirs? 3. When a farmer dictated in 1902 that women were excluded from inheriting his farms, little did he know that a century later, his great grand-daughters would stand up for their rights. ___________________________________________________________________________________________________________________________________________________________ Invoicing Back references from Insert ID in Invoice: Title Author Last Updated Invoice for Absolute right of inheritance (5623) Annalise Lubbe 10 February 2020

metadata.One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...): Private wills will come under the spotlight in a ‘world first’ matter when the ConCourt have to decide on the ‘absolute right of inheritance’ for adopted children and ‘male only’ heirs. We
metadata.Unique Selling Point: Private wills – as opposed to charitable trusts – are considered sacrosanct, not only in South Africa but the world over. As long as a person is of “sound mind” and not financially responsible for any minor children, they are legally entitled to pass on their assets to whoever they please and can disinherit on a whim. But in a constitutional dispensation this is not an “absolute right” and must be balanced against equality, it has been argued in two matters that will now come before the Constitutional Court in February.
metadata.Summary: The first case involves the inheritance rights of adult adoptees. In the other, five sisters have challenged a “males only” clause in their great-grandfather’s will. Both challenges started in the Cape Town high court, but were unsuccessful. Then the Supreme Court of Appeal (SCA) failed to come to their aid. But the ConCourt has consolidated the two cases and directed the parties to submit arguments on why it should grant leave to appeal as well as the merits of both matters. There are very few grounds on which to challenge a private will in South Africa (and in fact worldwide). Essentially a person can leave their money and property to whoever they want. Usually challenges are made on allegations that the person was unduly influenced, or was not sane at the time of writing the will. But, as far as we know - and what the papers say in these two matters - the “constitutionality” of a private will has never been tested before. The argument in both these cases is that the right of someone to leave their money to whoever they wish is not “absolute” and should be balanced against equality provisions in the Bill of Rights and the Constitution.
metadata.Further information: Adopted children case: David Wilkinson and his sister Amanda Truter are from Port Elizabeth. Dulcie Harper, who was unable to have children, adopted them as newborns in the 1950s. In 1953, before Harper adopted the babies, her father Louis John Druiff died. In a trust deed and will, Druiff left his estate in equal shares to his four children and, on their deaths, their children. Harper died in December 2017. She was the last of Druiff’s four children to die. Her death sparked a legal battle between Wilkinson and Truter and their cousins about who was entitled to inherit Harper’s share of her father’s estate. The cousins, the natural children of Harper’s siblings, claimed that Wilkinson and Truter, as adopted children, were not entitled to the inheritance because Druiff only intended “blood descendents” to inherit. Wilkinson and Truter argued that this interpretation was incorrect, resulted in unfair discrimination and was not in line with the “spirit, purpose and object of the bill of rights and the constitution”. The appeal court judges were divided. Judge Mahube Betty Molemela said in a minority judgment that Druiff had used the term “any child”. There was no reason why this should lead to the conclusion that he intended to disinherit children adopted after his death. She noted that Druiff was aware, before his death, that Harper was considering adoption. But the majority judgment, penned by judge Visvanathan Ponnan, highlighted the constitution's protection of a person’s right to property, including the right to dispose of their assets as they wish upon their death. “The fundamental question is the extent to which freedom of testation must yield to freedom from unfair discrimination,” the judges said. “Inroads into freedom of testation are not to be made lightly. No one has a right to inherit. The terms of the trust deed were certain and valid and not contrary to public policy at the time.” The adopted siblings’ lawyers said the case raises “important constitutional issues". "The net result is that adopted children are being discriminated against solely on the basis of their birth and status, which is a contravention of the constitution … There is no authoritative pronouncement on the issue. None of the authorities deal with private trust in the present constitutional dispensation,” they said. They argued that the appeal court failed to take into account “radical developments of law” concerning adopted children and that “public policy” is not a static concept. “Any finding which results in adoptive children not being on equal footing would today fall foul of public policy and the equality clause in the constitution.” Wilkinson and Truter are adopted children (now adults) of Harper who want to claim from her fathers’ (Druiff) estate. In his will he provided that his children and their children can inherit. In the Western Cape High Court, the court ruled against them as did the majority of judges in the SCA. They highlighted the protection of the Constitution of a person's right to property including the right to dispose of their assets as they wish upon their death. “The fundamental question is the extent to which freedom of testation, must yield to freedom from unfair discrimination,” they said. “Inroads into freedom of testation are not to be made lightly. Noone has a right to inherit. The terms of the trust deed were certain and valid and not contrary to public policy at the time.” But in a minority judgment, Judge Mahube Molemela, aid Druiff had used the term “any child”. There was no reason why this should lead to the conclusion that he intended to disinherit children adopted after his own death. It was this minority judgment that led to the Legal Aid Board taking up the case on behalf of adopted children on appeal to the Constitutional Court. They had run out of money and were not going to pursue it. I would guess from that, that the Legal Aid Board believes it has a strong case and one which is deserving of Concourt scrutiny. Lawyers acting for the adopted siblings, have submitted the case raises “important Constitutional issues”. They say: “The net result is that adopted children are being discriminated against solely on the basis of their birth and status which is a contravention of the Constitution. “There is no authoritative pronouncement on the issue. None of the authorities deal with private trust in the present Constitutional dispensation. “ They argue that the SCA failed to take into account “radical developments of law” concerning adopted children and that “public policy” is not a static concept. “Any finding which results in adoptive children not being on equal footing would today fall foul of public policy and the equality clause in the Constitution.” This case really comes down to interpretation of a will (which did not specifically preclude adopted children) but even if it did, is that permissible today? The “men only” case In the second matter, sisters Trudene Forword, Annelie Jordaan, Elna Slabber, Kalene Roux and Surina Serfontein claimed unfair discrimination after being disinherited because the will their great-grandparents drafted in 1902 specified that only “male heirs” could inherit their farms and other properties. Their father Kalvyn de Jager died in 2015 having had only daughters. Their male cousins then laid claim to the properties, admitting that it may be “unfair discrimination” but that it is justified and “freedom of testation should take precedence”. In written arguments, lawyers for the sisters said a will that is inimical (obstruct, unfriendly) to constitutional values, that is contrary to public policy, is not enforceable. “While the law of succession offers a testator very wide freedom, this is limited by common law, statute and the constitution," they argued. “For example, if a property owner were to conclude a contract with an estate agent which permits the agent to only market and sell the property to persons of a particular race or gender, it stands to reason that such contract would be unenforceable on the basis of breach of public policy. “If there is to be a blanket acceptance that freedom of testation trumps equality in all cases of out-and-out disinheritance, the result would be a ‘constitution-free zone’ created under the guise of freedom to testation.” But lawyers for the cousins say neither the interim constitution nor the final constitution reaches backwards to invalidate actions taken before they commenced. “It is significant that at the Supreme Court of Appeal, the counsel [for the sisters] had to concede that they are contending for a ‘world first’ in the sense that no foreign jurisdiction has outlawed discrimination in the form of out-and-out disinheritance in a private will.” They also argued that this was not the case to decide a constitutional issue. “Over the past 117 years, the family has arranged their affairs in accordance with the will,” they said. “Some of the properties have been sold - it will be difficult to unscramble these transactions.” They said their clients were not able to justify the discrimination because of the passage of time and that it was impossible to establish what benefits were distributed to females in lieu of property in the past. “There is also the spectre of a Pandora’s box of litigation regarding private wills, in which the testators’ last wishes are second-guessed by a court, which might have little inkling as to why,” they said. The five sisters are challenging their grand grandfathers will which left properties only to male sheirs (back in 1902). Their father only had girls (them) so they are now disinherited because of that and their male cousins stand to gain (the male children of their uncle). They lost in the Western Cape High Court and the SCA did not grant leave to appeal (no reasons). This case is probably less winnable. While it might be contrary to public policy and the constitution in the present day, it wasn’t back then. But the court may pronounce on this issue without fiddling with the terms of the will - ie it may say that in the present day this would be unconstitutional meaning that a present day testator may have to be more cautious about who he leaves his money to - and may have to give sound reasons for disinheritance - in order to avoid a “constitutional challenge” by disgruntled potential heirs. So either way they are important matters. The court has issued directions that argument in both matters be filed on the leave to appeal issue and the merits. So that means both will be argued. It is possible that after hearing both, they may not grant leave to appeal! But that essentially means that they are not interested in addressing the merits of the matter. But my sense is they want to rule - one way or another - on the Constitutionality issue.
